recall_prompt: Say how you would find this sum — how you rewrite the bracket as a series in 1/100, what you compare with, how you find p, q and x, what the bracket comes to, and what the 7/5 does at the end.
insider_note: The powers 1/10², 1/10⁴, 1/10⁶ make the common ratio 1/100, not 1/10. The 7/5 outside the bracket is there to cancel the 5/7 in S — the final answer is exactly √2.

steps.label: Rewrite with factorials
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Each denominator is a product like 5·10·15 = 5³·(1·2·3), so every term becomes (a product)/(k!) times (1/100)ᵏ. Work on the bracket S alone and multiply by 7/5 at the end. 1/10², 1/10⁴, 1/10⁶ are (1/100)¹, (1/100)², (1/100)³, so the common ratio is 1/100.

recall.must_convey: That the series is rewritten so the k-th term is a product over k! times (1/100) to the power k.
accept: write each term as a product over k factorial times one by hundred to the power k
split each denominator into hundred to the power k times k factorial
bring the series to the shape one plus p by one factorial into x by q and so on
prathi term ni k factorial tho, one by hundred power k tho rayali
rewrite the denominators as powers of hundred times factorials

steps.why: The standard expansion of (1 − x)^(−p/q) has a k! in every denominator and a fixed ratio x/q raised to k. Until the given series is written in that exact shape, p, q and x cannot be read off.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add the missing terms on both sides when the series starts late, so the comparison has no 1 to match.
Writing 5·10·15 as 5·3! instead of 5³·3! — every factor carries a 100.
Losing the alternating sign when the terms alternate.

steps.label: Compare with the standard expansion
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for WRITING the standard expansion beside the series. The examiner looks for the pattern p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!. All plus signs mean the (1 − x) form.

recall.must_convey: That the series is compared with the expansion of (1 − x) to the power minus p by q, whose coefficients are p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!.
accept: compare with the expansion of (1 − x) to the power minus p by q
match it with one plus p by one factorial into x by q plus p into p plus q by two factorial into x by q squared and so on
use the standard binomial series with negative fractional index (1 − x) to the power minus p by q
(1 − x)^(−p/q) formula tho compare cheyali
the pattern p then p into p plus q over the factorials is the standard series

steps.why: This is the only binomial expansion whose coefficients grow as p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q). Naming it turns the rest of the question into reading off three numbers.
common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form for an alternating series or the (1 + x) form for an all-plus series.
Writing p(p + 1) instead of p(p + q) — the step between factors is q, not 1.

steps.label: Find p, q and x
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. p is the first factor (1), p + q is the second (3) so q = 2, and x/q equals the common ratio 1/100 so x = q/100 = 2/100 = 1/50.

recall.must_convey: That p = 1 and p + q = 3 give q = 2, and x/q = 1/100 gives x = one by fifty.
accept: p is one, p plus q is three so q is two, and x by q is one by hundred so x is one by fifty
the first factor gives p equal to one and the second gives q equal to two
x by q equals one by hundred so x equals one by fifty
p one, q two vasthai, x by q one by hundred kabatti x one by fifty
read off p from the first numerator and q from the gap between the factors

steps.why: Three unknowns need three matches: the first numerator fixes p, the second fixes p + q, and the ratio inside the bracket fixes x/q. Nothing else in the series is free.
common_mistakes: Taking x = 1/100 directly — the bracket holds x/q, so x = q × 1/100.
Reading q from the second factor as a whole instead of as p + q.

steps.label: Evaluate the power
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Substitute p, q, x into (1 − x)^(−p/q) and simplify the fraction inside the bracket before touching the exponent.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives root of fifty by forty nine, which is five root two by seven.
accept: substituting gives root of fifty by forty nine, which is five root two by seven
put the values into (1 − x)^(−p/q) and simplify to get root of fifty by forty nine, which is five root two by seven
the bracket becomes forty nine by fifty and the power gives root of fifty by forty nine, which is five root two by seven
values substitute cheste root of fifty by forty nine, which is five root two by seven vasthundi
simplify the bracket first then apply the negative index
heard_as: root of fifty by forty nine, which is five root two by seven

steps.why: A negative index inverts the fraction and a fractional index takes a root. Doing the inversion first keeps the root over a simple fraction.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exponent instead of the fraction when the index is negative.
Leaving a root in the denominator without a clear final value.

steps.label: Multiply by 7/5
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The 7/5 outside the bracket was chosen to cancel the 5/7 in S — the 7s cancel, the 5s cancel, and √2 is left.

recall.must_convey: That the given series is 7/5 times S, and 7/5 times 5√2/7 is √2.

steps.why: The bracket is the whole series; the 7/5 is a constant factor that stays outside until the bracket is known.
common_mistakes: Taking the common ratio as 1/10 instead of 1/100.
